note: Curated milestones in the pursuit of pi, rendered by js/timeline.js. Sort keys are years; negative means BCE. Eras are bands over the sort key; each milestone falls into the last era whose start it passes. Sources for every entry are cited in atlas chapter 02.

eras.title: Rope, clay, and papyrus
eras.lede: Before proofs there were measurements. Builders and scribes needed a working number for the circle, and the guesses they carved into clay were already startlingly close.

eras.title: The geometers
eras.lede: Archimedes turned estimation into mathematics: trap the circle between polygons and squeeze. For eighteen centuries, every improvement on four continents was someone squeezing harder.

eras.title: The infinite arrives
eras.lede: In Kerala, and later in Europe, the circle met the infinite series. Suddenly pi was not something you measured. It was something you could summon, term by term, forever.

eras.title: The name and the proofs
eras.lede: The number finally got its letter, then its character: never a fraction, never the root of any polynomial. The dream of squaring the circle died in 1882, in four pages of German.

eras.title: Genius and silicon
eras.lede: Ramanujan wrote series that gain eight digits a term. Then the machines arrived, and a constant that took a lifetime to know to 35 places fell by thousands of digits in an afternoon.

eras.title: The trillion era
eras.lede: Pi became the benchmark of the computing world: the number every record-hungry machine gets pointed at. The frontier now moves by hundreds of trillions of digits at a time.

milestones.what: A clay tablet implies pi is about 25/8 = 3.125, the earliest known estimate.
A circle's area is computed as if pi were (16/9) squared, about 3.1605.
Traps pi between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 using 96-sided polygons, the first rigorous method.
Uses 377/120, about 3.1416, in the Almagest for astronomy.
Publishes a polygon algorithm with error control and reaches 3.1416.
Pins pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927 and offers 355/113, unmatched for over 900 years.
Gives 3.1416 and calls it approaching, a hint that the value is never exact.
Discovers the arctangent series centuries before Europe and computes about 11 digits.
Computes 2 pi to 9 sexagesimal places, 16 decimal digits, a record for nearly two centuries.
Writes pi as an infinite product of nested square roots, the first exact formula.
Spends decades on polygons to reach 35 digits, later engraved on his tombstone.
Finds pi/2 as an infinite product of whole-number ratios, before calculus.
The arctangent series reaches Europe: pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 and so on.
A clever arctangent identity yields 100 digits, the method of record for two centuries.
First uses the Greek letter pi for the ratio, in Synopsis Palmariorum Matheseos.
Adopts the symbol pi in his Introductio and makes it universal.
Proves pi is irrational: its digits can never repeat.
Publishes 707 hand-computed digits. Only 527 are right, but nobody notices for 71 years.
Proves pi is transcendental, settling 2,000 years of circle squaring in the negative.
House Bill 246 nearly legislates a wrong value of pi. The Senate quietly shelves it.
Publishes series that gain about 8 digits per term, decades ahead of their time.
The first computer calculation: 2,037 digits in about 70 hours.
100,265 digits on an IBM 7090, the first six-figure count.

milestones.who: Jean Guilloud and Martine Bouyer, France
milestones.what: Pass one million digits on a CDC 7600.
Publish the series behind every record since: 14 new digits per term.
A formula that extracts any hexadecimal digit of pi without the ones before it.
1.24 trillion digits on a Hitachi supercomputer.
2.7 trillion digits on a single desktop PC, beating supercomputers on cost.
5 trillion digits at home with y-cruncher, the software behind every record since.
31.4 trillion digits in the cloud, announced on Pi Day.
100 trillion digits, more than tripling her own 2019 record.
105 trillion digits in March, then 202 trillion in June.
300 trillion digits, verified as a Guinness World Record.
314 trillion digits on one server in 110 days. The record as this site went live.
